title: Introducing Tinfoil Bunkers
summary: Tinfoil Bunkers are a confidential home for AI agents, experiments, and interactive work, with verifiable privacy, persistent storage, and credential isolation through your Perimeter.
body_markdown:
[Back to posts](https://tinfoil.sh/blog)


# Introducing Tinfoil Bunkers


Nov 12, 2026


•


14 min read


Mia Korennykh


We’re excited to introduce[Tinfoil Bunkers](https://tinfoil.sh/bunkers) , a confidential home for running highly customized workflows such as AI agents, experiments, and interactive work, all with the same verifiable privacy and transparency guarantees offered to you by our other products.


## Bunkers are a true extension of your personal computer


Bunkers act as an extension of your personal computer, where you can put anything you would have or run locally into a confidential cloud environment that’s separate from your computer and always running. It’s a new approach for personal and agentic computing and we’re really excited to be pushing the frontier for privacy here.


Tinfoil Bunkers offer:


- **A home for your agents** — Bunkers are always running, even when your computer is off, with an expansive built-in software library (powered by Nix!), and are built to keep your data for as long as you need.
- **Confidentiality** — Bunkers are fully confidential and were built to withstand compromised infrastructure. Every Tinfoil Bunker runs in its own secure enclave, with memory encryption and isolation boundaries handled by AMD and Intel microarchitecture. Nobody, not Tinfoil or anyone else, can see inside a Bunker. Bunkers verify this end-to-end before you connect, like all confidential Tinfoil products.
- **Access control and credential isolation** — While privacy from the host is great, a rogue agent or workload compromise can pose an even larger immediate risk. Agents today often run with full possession over their credentials, often without any guardrails (` --dangerously-skip-permissions` ,` --yolo` ). There are certain approaches, such as using other LLMs to monitor agent work, which have been the default answer until now, but they don’t give us a model to reason about what a Bunker can or cannot do. The Bunker’s Perimeter, in contrast to these approaches, lets you keep secrets out of reach of your Bunkers, and allows for peace of mind while giving your agents access.


## Try Bunkers now


Stop reading this. Bunkers are best experienced firsthand.[Try making one!](https://dash.tinfoil.sh/?tab=sandboxes) Once one is set up, try adding a connector. You can set a policy and give agents access, and verify that anything you didn’t authorize gets blocked.


Once you’ve come back: or if you want to examine the architecture of these more closely before you use them :) (nice tinfoil hat![We’re hiring](https://tinfoil.sh/join-us) ) then follow along. The rest of the blog will cover the considerations, the threat model, and in-depth discussion of how we designed these to be as secure and user friendly as possible (and yes these are actually not complete opposites, because the more secure your credentials are from the agent the less you have to worry).


## Why we built Bunkers


OpenClaw was cool. Personal intelligence is good. Personal intelligence needs files, it needs access, it needs a home. This can’t always be your computer.


On a more serious note, AI has taken over a lot of our lives. As the tech starts to know more about us personally and act on our behalf, private gardens for thought are becoming more scarce and isolated. We think that personal assistants are going to be as deeply embedded in human life as they did with smartphones. Unlike the smartphone revolution, this one doesn’t have any privacy to speak of. We need to find ways of preserving privacy as personal assistants mature. We started with offering the best available intelligence privately. Now, as that intelligence is embodied, and gets better at acting, it needs a place to act & do on your behalf. For this we’re making a private extension of your computer.


Simultaneously, the recent cybersecurity climate has been very eventful to say the least. Cloud breaches were previously assumed to only be within reach of nation-state actors, but now anyone pointing a model at the right repo with the right prompt can just look inside. Confidential computing is unusually well equipped for this! Since the entire execution context that a workload is running in is encrypted, a VM escape vulnerability or host compromise cannot expose any information about anyone’s workloads being run on the machine, taking Tinfoil and cloud providers out of the trust boundary.[Tinfoil Containers](https://tinfoil.sh/containers) made this accessible to anyone trying to run an existing workload, and Bunkers are built on top of it.


## Why might you use a Bunker?


Bunkers are perfect when you want to run a workload in the cloud but keep the privacy of your personal computer. Any time you think of using cloud VMs is also a reason to use a Bunker, but you get guaranteed privacy as well. That is, uninterrupted processing, more compute than you have on hand, somewhere to experiment with risky things, a place to run your agents, or to build a second brain — all without needing to keep your laptop open. The sky’s really the limit here. It’s a computer.


## Threat model: Setting a new standard for isolating workloads


There are currently two kinds of attacks which concern Bunker workloads: stopping an attacker from getting in, and preventing an agent from breaking out.


### Stopping an attacker from getting in


All of our TCB is fully reproducible and auditable, and we have spent a lot of time on minimizing the attack surface available for the host to perform on workloads.


In the previous blog post,[Less is More](https://tinfoil.sh/blog/2026-10-25-less-is-more) , we detailed how we were able to eliminate 300 MB of OVMF boot firmware for an extremely minimal, 513-line bootloader purpose-built for starting CVMs. Firmware is especially important because it is privileged code which determines the entire future state of the enclave, so an attack at that level would compromise the guarantees an attestation is supposed to make.


We use this new lighter firmware in our Bunker product, and it lets us make a new kind of argument we weren’t able to before, but is very important for Bunkers: one Bunker should never be able to impersonate another. All Bunker enclaves boot the same stable cvmimage release, but the measured image is parameterized at boot time with a config which differs from enclave to enclave. Since a user’s key is bound directly inside of the config, it is both impossible for anyone else to access it, and for anyone to maliciously impersonate it as one of the enclaves you control.


Attacks on container runtimes have become increasingly common in the past year. In light of this news, the industry has started turning to MicroVM solutions such as[Firecracker](https://firecracker-microvm.github.io/) or[gVisor](https://gvisor.dev/) as a stronger security boundary. Despite improving kernel isolation, host escapes still happen, letting sophisticated attackers breach every VM running on a system. Given the rising rate of autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation, infrastructure is becoming increasingly less trustworthy. A few months ago, OpenAI reported that an RL environment had been escaped, hacking into several organizations in pursuit of answers for an eval run.1 We believe that all infrastructure will be a prevalent point of failure eventually, and the best solution is to build a cloud that requires as little trust as possible.


### Stopping agents from breaking out


We don’t think it’s fair to say a Bunker is truly private or trustworthy unless we’ve somehow solved this. The problem is that to meaningfully define what level of access a Bunker has, we can’t let it have real credentials, otherwise any way to exfiltrate it would lead to ambient access you cannot see. Inspired by progress in workload authorization, we instead give the Bunker just a single credential: its identity. Then, in the event of a breach the Perimeter can revoke access, and that’s that.


Wherever software expects a token, we instead provide a fake one, that the AI or software can use, and substitute it on the way out. This has slightly more nuance to it than might seem at first glance: authorization works differently on different websites, and we want to avoid fatal mistakes like, for instance, an agent emailing its own password, and then the Perimeter substituting in the real one once it’s sent out.


To handle edge cases like this, we’re shipping an expansive set of presets describing various services you might want to connect to, where credentials are expected to exist, and what the general behavior of a platform looks like. If a credential is attempted to be used in an unexpected place, it instantly gets rejected. This is better than the naive case, where generally it’s a user’s job to configure their services correctly. The Perimeter supports 100+ common APIs and MCP servers out of the box, and you can proxy common protocols such as SSH, IMAP, and Postgres out of the box. Since we have knowledge of how each service works, we can let users generally set policies like only allowing read-only access, or block all payments.


It is easy to see the challenges of access control immediately being an issue with SSH: what appears at first to be a simple proxying mechanism can still lead to compromise if the machine being connected to contains credentials that can then be used maliciously later. We instead handle these in layers: TCP traffic gets its own facts, where access control can be applied such as acceptable domains etc., while the SSH connector is able to do credential substitution and block things such as file transfers. An even deeper integration can, for example, parse or screen shell commands and then execute them on the target host in a more structured form. We can use these policies to deterministically replay and explain why a judgment is made, and run policies on past history. We believe that these properties give us a model for Bunker behavior that captures enough granularity to prevent attacks.


### Passkeys


You’ll notice that when using Bunkers, you never have to provide an SSH key. This is because we use passkeys, using an approach similar to what we currently do for Tinfoil Chat. Whenever a Bunker is being created, we redirect you to an open-source webapp known as[Tinfoil Terminal](https://terminal.tinfoil.sh/) . That is the only domain where keys are unlocked, and we intentionally enforce this split to minimize what you have to trust. In that environment, we generate new SSH keys, and encrypt them under your PRF (which can be something like a system-level key, or a Yubikey). The CLI and other devices can access that same data at a later time, allowing for seamless access to your Bunkers without any complex key management.


If you prefer to bring your own keys, the dashboard allows you to choose a CLI-only mode. This makes it impossible to access through the web terminal, but keeps the private key completely under custody of your` ssh-agent` .


### Complete isolation


We’re pursuing complete isolation. Many coding harnesses use process isolation: on your computer the environment that does the execution is a separate, isolated process. However, there have been times where this isn’t good enough. Processes can be escaped. For true isolation, we put the Perimeter in a separate Confidential VM (CVM) than the Bunker’s CVM, and the Bunker’s network is restricted, from the outside, to only go through the Perimeter. This has the fun consequence that every time you SSH into the Bunker you have to go through the Perimeter because it literally cannot be reached outside of it.


Noisy neighbor leakage and observing microarchitecture-level behavior side channels tends to be unavoidable for most multi-tenant applications. Even if two VMs are separate, giving one arbitrary code execution puts a real stress test on how much information can be recovered from carrying out long-term observation on the machine. Since the Perimeter is its own CVM, we can harden against this: we put all Perimeters in a completely different physical set of hosts from any other workload that’s running. Even in the worst case of Bunkers being able to side channel other Bunkers, no secrets can ever be stolen, because they live in an entirely separate environment.


This also means that the Perimeter’s log of what happens in the Bunker is very hard to tamper with or change. Taking care of these factors gives us the confidence to have agents explore and try out things in the Bunker.


## Bunker building blocks


### Containers


Previously, we had Containers, which were stateless. We made the following improvements that made Bunkers possible:


- **Firmware and private configs** : It’s now possible to dynamically configure a workload at launch time, letting you set variables dynamically which are measured and then attest to it.
- **Persistent volumes** : Most Tinfoil workloads, such as inference or training environments, are stateless. We now have encrypted volumes for persistent state.
- **Network isolation** : You can now isolate a workload from the rest of the internet, and map containers to stable LAN IPs.


### Persistence


For confidential production workloads, statelessness is the gold standard as a hardening measure. The fewer interactions a VM has with a host, the easier it is to reason about and reduce TCB. When given the option, a product or protocol should be redesigned around this principle. For long-running agents, experiments, and your files, however, you need an encrypted disk. We had to think a lot about reducing the attack surface and mitigating threats such as side channels, since this was the first time we offer a solution for persistent workloads.


A common footgun that can happen when in a confidential setting is using LUKS directly, which embeds a lot of metadata on the algorithm and parameters of the cryptography being used. We can avoid this by just using dm-crypt and dm-integrity directly, and initialize it with fixed values. Any host-controlled source of configuration parameters is intrinsically untrustworthy. As for side channels, Red Hat discussed in an article and a recent talk that side channels correlating a history of disk ciphertexts over a deterministic IV and known block layouts can reveal plaintexts in cases such as database writes and repeated accesses in object storage.2 Fortunately, dm-crypt allows us to mitigate this by using a randomized IV mode (as opposed to plain mode) for AES-XTS at the cost of some performance and disk overhead.


With this setup, we are able to reuse well-audited Linux security components, and also allow for high-throughput disk writes.


It’s important to note that access pattern correlation is not covered under this model, as they apply just as equally to CVM RAM. Protections against this can be implemented at an application level on top of a volume with performance depending on your workload. As an example of one such implementation and a detailed study of the tradeoffs, see[Opal](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02522) , a private memory system for personal AI built on Tinfoil.


### A feature-rich userspace


We also built Bunkers with an extremely intuitive user experience in mind. To this end, we chose to leverage Nix, plus a clever trick Replit came up with a few years ago known as[Supercolliding Nix stores](https://blog.replit.com/super-colliding-nix-stores) . A significant benefit of Nix is that software packaging is hermetic and reproducible across all builds, which allows a persistent Bunker to overlay its own persistent view of installed software on top of a larger, potentially remote external store with no risk of conflicting versions and builds. In Replit’s case, the store can be as large as 2 TB! With Tinfoil, this means Bunkers are built as thin images that mount over a large immutable store, and most common development software available in Nix is ready to go instantly. Harnesses are configured to connect through Tinfoil out of the box.


## Future work


We will continue iterating and implementing more connectors to the Perimeter in the coming weeks. With Bunkers/Perimeter we hope to bring a useful product: personal desktop extensions. Along the way we uncovered and built lots of primitives, and we are excited to see this used by everyone for private agents. We believe that private AI is essential for preserving personal agency far into the future.
